title: Power to Your Home
blurb: You press a switch and the light comes on. But how does electricity travel from a power station to your room?

chapters.title: What Is Electricity?
chapters.text:
Everything around us is made of tiny particles called atoms. Inside atoms there are even smaller particles called electrons, which carry a negative electric charge. In some materials, such as copper, electrons can move easily from one atom to the next. We call these materials conductors.

When a large number of electrons flow in the same direction through a wire, we say that an electric current is flowing. Electric current is not something that you can see, but you can see what it does: it lights a bulb, spins a fan or heats a kettle.

Materials such as plastic, rubber and glass hold their electrons tightly. They are called insulators, and they do not let current pass. That is why electric wires have a plastic coat. The metal inside carries the current, and the plastic keeps you safe.

questions.why: Materials such as copper are conductors.

chapters.title: Making Electricity
chapters.text:
In a power station, electricity is made by a machine called a generator. A generator contains a strong magnet and a coil of copper wire. When the magnet spins next to the coil, it pushes the electrons in the wire and a current begins to flow. This was discovered by a scientist called Michael Faraday in 1831.

Something must spin the magnet. Usually, it is a turbine, which is a wheel with blades like a very large fan. In many power stations, steam turns the turbine. The steam is made by boiling water with heat from burning coal or gas.

In a hydroelectric station, falling water spins the turbine. In a wind farm, the wind does it. In a geothermal power station, steam comes from hot rocks deep underground. Indonesia has many volcanoes, so it has a lot of hot rock, and geothermal energy is an important source there.

chapters.title: Up the Wires
chapters.text:
After the electricity is made, it must travel to towns and cities that may be hundreds of kilometres away. It travels along thick metal cables carried by tall steel towers. There is a problem, however. As current flows through a long wire, some of the energy turns into heat and is lost. The bigger the current, the more energy is wasted.

Engineers solve the problem with a clever machine called a transformer. A step-up transformer at the power station raises the voltage to a very high level, such as 150,000 volts. When the voltage is high, the current needed to carry the same power is smaller, so less energy is lost as heat.

This is why we see warning signs on tall towers. Very high voltage is dangerous, and nobody should climb near the cables.

chapters.title: Cities and Substations
chapters.text:
Before electricity can be used at home, the voltage must come down again. Near the city, the cables enter a substation, which is a fenced area with large machines. Here, step-down transformers lower the voltage in stages.

The electricity then runs along smaller cables and wires on poles along the street. Near your house, a last small transformer reduces the voltage to 230 volts, which is the voltage used in homes in Indonesia.

Islands need special solutions. In places where islands are close to each other, cables are laid on the sea floor to carry electricity across the water. For example, there is an undersea cable between Java and Bali. In remote villages without a cable, solar panels or small generators supply power.

chapters.title: Inside Your Home
chapters.text:
The electricity enters your home through a meter, which measures how much you use, and then goes to a box with switches called circuit breakers. From there, wires run inside the walls to sockets and lights.

For a lamp to work, the current must have a complete path, called a circuit. It leaves the supply, passes through the lamp and returns. When you press a switch, you open or close a gap in the circuit. A closed circuit lets current flow, and an open circuit stops it.

Circuit breakers keep you safe. If too much current flows, perhaps because a wire has been damaged, the breaker switches itself off and cuts the circuit. Remember these safety rules: never put anything but a plug into a socket, keep water away from sockets, and never touch a damaged wire.

chapters.title: Power for Tomorrow
chapters.text:
Today, many power stations burn coal and gas, which release carbon dioxide. This gas traps heat in the air and contributes to climate change. So scientists and engineers are looking for cleaner ways to make electricity.

Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. They are very useful in sunny countries like Indonesia, and they can be placed on roofs. Wind turbines and hydro stations make power without burning fuel. Geothermal power stations use the Earth's own heat.

But the cleanest energy of all is the energy that we do not use. Switching off lights when you leave a room, choosing efficient bulbs and unplugging chargers all help. If every family saved a little, the power stations would have to burn less fuel, and the air would be cleaner for everyone.
